results.answer:
For days 61 through 75 of your stay, you'd pay **$434 per day**. During a benefit period, what you pay depends on how long you're getting inpatient hospital care:

- Days 1–60: After you pay the $1,736 Part A deductible, you pay $0 each day.
- Days 61–90: You pay $434 each day.

For a 75-day stay, that's 15 days at $434, or **$6,510**, plus the **$1,736** deductible. The deductible figure is listed as the amount (in 2026). Since your stay ends before day 91, you won't use any lifetime reserve days.

results.answer:
As a federal retiree with an OPM annuity who isn't entitled to Social Security or RRB benefits, you must ask to have your Part B premiums deducted from your annuity. Contact your local Social Security office to make your request. Visit SSA.gov/locator to find your local office.

If you don't set up that deduction, you'll get a bill for your Part B premium. Typically, Part B premiums are billed quarterly (every 3 months). There are 4 ways to pay your premium bill, including:

- Online through your secure Medicare account: Visit Medicare.gov/account to log into (or create) your Medicare account. Then, select "Pay my premium" to make a payment by credit card, debit card, Health Savings Account (HSA) card, or from your checking or savings account. This free service is the fastest way to pay your premium.
- Medicare Easy Pay, a free service that automatically deducts your payment. If you use it, you'll get a monthly bill.

The excerpts provided don't list the remaining two payment methods.

results.answer:
No deductible applies. Basic Option does not have a calendar year deductible. Instead, most services are subject to copayments ($35 for primary care providers and $50 for specialists).

For a Self Only enrollment, your out-of-pocket maximum for eligible coinsurance and copayment amounts is **$7,500** when you use Preferred providers. Only eligible expenses for Preferred provider services count toward these limits. When your eligible out-of-pocket expenses reach this catastrophic protection maximum, you no longer have to pay the associated cost-sharing amounts for the rest of the calendar year.

Keep in mind:
- Some expenses are not included under this feature. These expenses do not count toward your catastrophic protection out-of-pocket maximum, and you must continue to pay them even after you reach it.
- Under Basic Option you must use Preferred providers in order to receive benefits. There are no benefits for care performed by Participating and Non-participating providers. The exceptions include cases like medical emergency or accidental injury.

results.answer:
Under Original Medicare, day 45 falls in the second tier of a skilled nursing facility benefit period:

- Days 21–100: You pay $217 each day.

results.answer:
Completing the Blue Health Assessment (BHA) gets you a personalized health plan, access to goal-based rewards, and possibly a free blood pressure monitor.

**Health plan and coaching**
- The BHA is an online health evaluation which can be completed in 10-20 minutes.
- Your BHA answers are evaluated to create a unique health action plan.
- Based on the results, you can select personalized goals, receive supportive advice, and track your progress through the online coaching tool, Daily Habits.

**Health account dollars**
- $40 is added to your health account for each goal achieved, up to a maximum of three goals per year.
- By completing the BHA and a maximum of three health goals, you can earn up to a total of **$170** in health account dollars. The documents don't state the BHA's own reward separately.
- You must complete the BHA and your selected goals during the calendar year to receive these incentives.
- Only certain goals count. They must relate to exercise, nutrition, weight management, stress, emotional health, heart disease, heart failure, hypertension, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and asthma.

**Free blood pressure monitor (hypertension)**
If you have hypertension, you can qualify for a free blood pressure monitor (BPM). This program is available to the contract holder and spouse. You qualify when both of these are true:
- You complete the BHA and indicate that you have been diagnosed with hypertension.
- At least one medical claim has been processed during the past 12 months with a reported diagnosis of hypertension.

results.answer:
To place your first mail-order prescription through the Mail Service Prescription Drug Program:

- Complete the initial mail order form;
- Enclose your prescription and copayment;
- Mail your order to CVS Caremark, P.O. Box 1590, Pittsburgh, PA 15230-1590; and
- Allow up to two weeks for delivery.

Alternatively, your physician may call in your initial prescription at 800-262-7890, TTY: 711. You are responsible for the copayment.

Timing: expect **up to two weeks** for the first order. For comparison, you should allow up to ten days for delivery on refills.

Eligibility depends on your option:
- Standard Option: Standard Option members may use our Mail Service Prescription Drug Program to fill their prescriptions.
- Basic Option: The Mail Service Prescription Drug Program is available only to members with primary Medicare Part B coverage under Basic Option.

Other points that could affect your order:
- If your drug needs prior approval, the program will not fill it until you have that approval. CVS Caremark, the program administrator, will hold your prescription for you up to 30 days. If prior approval is not obtained within 30 days, your prescription will be unable to be filled and a letter will be mailed to you explaining the prior approval procedures.
- Specialty drugs will not be dispensed through the Mail Service Prescription Drug Program.

results.answer:
A doctor who doesn't accept assignment can charge **up to 15% above** the Medicare-approved amount. They can charge you more than the Medicare-approved amount. In many cases, the charge can't be more than 15% above the Medicare-approved amount for non-participating healthcare providers. This amount is called "the limiting charge." Put another way, such a physician may not bill you for more than 115% of the amount Medicare bases its payment on.

**Exception for opt-out doctors:** A doctor who has opted out of Medicare is different from a non-participating doctor. Should you visit an opt-out physician, the physician will not be limited to 115% of the Medicare-approved amount.

**If you're overcharged:** If your physician tries to collect more than allowed by law, ask the physician to reduce the charges. If the physician does not, report the physician to the Medicare carrier that sent you the MSN form.

results.answer:
Under Original Medicare, you appeal using your Medicare Summary Notice (MSN):

- Get the "Medicare Summary Notice" (MSN) that shows the item or service you're appealing.
- Circle the item(s) on the MSN you disagree with. Write an explanation of why you disagree with the decision. You can write on the MSN or on a separate piece of paper and attach it to the MSN.
- Include your name, phone number, and Medicare Number on the MSN. Keep a copy for your records.
- Send the MSN, or a copy, to the company that handles bills for Medicare (Medicare Administrative Contractor) listed on the MSN. You can include any information you have about your appeal, like information from your health care provider.

Instead of marking up the MSN, you can use Form CMS-20027. To get this form, visit Medicare.gov/basics/forms-publications-mailings/forms/appeals, or call 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227) to have a copy mailed to you.

Deadline and decision timing:
- You must file your appeal by the date in the MSN. If you missed the deadline for appealing, you may still file an appeal and get a decision if you can show good cause for missing the deadline.
- You'll generally get a decision from the Medicare Administrative Contractor within 60 days after they get your request. If Medicare will cover the item(s) or service(s), it will be listed on your next MSN.

It also helps to ask your doctor, supplier, or other health care provider for any information to make your appeal stronger. Keep a copy of everything related to your appeal. You can also get help filing an appeal from your State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP).

results.answer:
The yearly Part B deductible is **$283 in 2026**. Under Original Medicare, if the Part B deductible applies, you must pay all costs (up to the Medicare-approved amount) until you meet the yearly Part B deductible ($283 in 2026).

I can't reliably tell which Medigap plans pay it. The Medigap comparison chart includes a "Medicare Part B deductible" row, but the extracted text shows only 100% | 100% | 100%** 100%** with no plan labels, so the figures can't be matched to specific plans. In the chart, if a box is empty, it means that service isn't covered by that Medigap plan and you're responsible for paying the cost.

Two related notes from the same page:
- Plans K and L pay 100% of covered services for the rest of the calendar year after you meet your out-of-pocket yearly limit and your yearly Part B deductible ($283 in 2026).
- You can't buy Medigap Plans C or F if you became eligible for Medicare on or after January 1, 2020.

To confirm which plans cover the deductible, check the original chart on page 80 of Medicare & You, or Medicare.gov.

results.answer:
Generally, no. Under Basic Option you must use Preferred providers in order to receive benefits. There are no benefits for care performed by Participating and Non-participating providers. For example, for diabetic education or office visits with a Participating/Non-participating provider, You pay all charges.

There are some exceptions:

- **Emergency care:** You must use Preferred providers for your care to be eligible for benefits, except in certain circumstances, such as emergency care. The brochure says to see Section 3 for exceptions under What you must do to get covered care.
- **Overseas care:** The Basic Option requirement to use Preferred providers in order to receive benefits does not apply when you receive overseas care.
- **Some lab and diagnostic work:** In the lab, X-ray and diagnostic tests section, Basic Option members pay all charges for Participating/Non-participating providers (except as noted below). That note applies If your Preferred provider uses a Non-preferred laboratory or radiologist, but the rest of the note is cut off in this excerpt.

If you have Medicare and your physician does not participate with Medicare and is not in our Preferred network, under Basic Option - all charges are your responsibility.
